label: Cramér–Rao and Fisher information — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: Fisher information for a single observation may be computed as:
options: E[∂ℓ/∂θ], which is non-zero under regularity
items.explanation: Both forms in A are standard and agree under regularity. B has the wrong sign and drops the condition. C is the OBSERVED information — a number from one dataset, not the expected information the bound uses. D is wrong on the fact: the score has expectation zero under regularity, which is why its variance is the useful quantity.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₂₅ are iid Bernoulli(p) with p = 0.4. Give the Cramér–Rao bound for unbiased estimators of p, and say whether x̄ attains it.
options: 0.0096, and x̄ does not attain it
0.24, and x̄ does not attain it
items.explanation: I(p) = 1/(p(1−p)), so the bound is p(1−p)/n = (0.4)(0.6)/25 = 0.24/25 = 0.0096. And Var(x̄) = p(1−p)/n is exactly that, so x̄ is efficient. Option C forgets to divide by n.
items.check: Two parts: the number and the attainment verdict. 0.24 is p(1−p) before dividing by n — check the n is in there.

items.stem: Consider the Cramér–Rao bound and its conditions.
items.explanation: A is true — the squared derivative is the correct numerator for a function of θ. B is true, and is the general form that reduces to the standard one when b ≡ 0. C is false: the converse fails, as the exponential rate shows. D is true, and is why U(0,θ) is excluded.
statements: For T unbiased for g(θ), the bound is [g′(θ)]²/(nI(θ)).
For a biased T with bias b(θ), the bound is (1+b′(θ))²/(nI(θ)).
Every UMVUE attains the Cramér–Rao bound.
The bound requires the support of the density to be free of θ.

A.why: The derivative is squared; forgetting the square is the commonest error in the topic.

B.why: The general form. Setting b ≡ 0 recovers the standard statement.

C.why: The exponential rate's UMVUE has variance λ²/(n−2), strictly above the floor λ²/n.

D.why: A moving support breaks differentiation under the integral, and with it the whole derivation.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₁₆ are iid Poisson(λ) with λ = 4. Give Iₙ(λ) and the Cramér–Rao bound for unbiased estimators of λ.
items.explanation: I₁(λ) = 1/λ = 0.25, so Iₙ = n/λ = 16/4 = 4, and the bound is its reciprocal, 1/4 = 0.25. Note Var(x̄) = λ/n = 0.25 too, so x̄ attains it. Option B uses I₁ = λ rather than 1/λ.
items.check: The bound is the RECIPROCAL of the total information. If your two numbers are not reciprocals of each other, one of them is wrong.

items.stem: For which family does the Cramér–Rao bound fail to apply?
options: U(0,θ), because the support depends on θ
N(μ,σ²) with σ² known, because there are two parameters
Poisson(λ), because the data are discrete
items.explanation: Regularity requires the support to be free of the parameter, and for U(0,θ) it is not — so differentiation under the integral fails and the bound is unavailable. Discreteness is no obstacle (B is wrong; Poisson and Bernoulli are both standard applications), a bounded parameter space is fine provided θ is interior, and in D σ² is known so there is only one unknown parameter.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₃₆ are iid N(μ, σ²) with σ² = 9 known. Give Iₙ(μ) and the Cramér–Rao bound for unbiased estimators of μ.
items.explanation: I₁(μ) = 1/σ² = 1/9, so Iₙ = n/σ² = 36/9 = 4 and the bound is 1/4 = 0.25. That equals Var(X̄) = σ²/n = 9/36 = 0.25, so x̄ is efficient. Option C multiplies by σ² instead of dividing.
items.check: σ² = 9 is the variance, not the standard deviation. I₁ = 1/σ² = 1/9, not 1/3.

items.stem: Let T be an unbiased estimator of θ in a regular family.
items.explanation: A is false — the MLE's efficiency is an asymptotic statement; at finite n it may be biased and above the floor. B is true, and is the standard shortcut to a UMVUE. C is true, and is the exact attainment criterion. D is false: efficiency is CRLB/Var, which cannot exceed 1.
statements: The MLE attains the Cramér–Rao bound exactly for every sample size.
If an unbiased T attains the Cramér–Rao bound for every θ in the model, then T is the UMVUE of θ.
The bound is attained if and only if the score can be written as A(θ)[T − θ].
Efficiency e(T) = CRLB/Var(T) can exceed 1 for a very good estimator.

A.why: Asymptotic only. Var(θ̂) → 1/(nI(θ)); at finite n it generally sits above.

B.why: True under the stated regularity conditions when equality holds throughout the parameter space: no unbiased estimator can have lower variance at any θ. Equality at only one isolated parameter value would not establish a globally minimum-variance unbiased estimator.

C.why: The linear-score condition is exactly the equality case of the Cauchy–Schwarz step.

D.why: Var(T) ≥ CRLB, so the ratio is at most 1. A value above 1 means an arithmetic error.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₁₀ are iid Exponential with rate λ = 2. The UMVUE of λ is (n−1)/ΣX, with variance λ²/(n−2). Give the Cramér–Rao bound and the efficiency of the UMVUE.
items.explanation: I(λ) = 1/λ², so the bound is λ²/n = 4/10 = 0.4. The UMVUE's variance is λ²/(n−2) = 4/8 = 0.5. Efficiency is CRLB/Var = 0.4/0.5 = 0.8. The best unbiased estimator is only 80% efficient here, which is the point: a UMVUE need not sit on the floor.
items.check: Efficiency is bound ÷ variance, so it must come out at or below 1. Option C's 1.25 is the ratio taken upside down.

items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Exponential with mean θ, so f(x) = (1/θ)e^(−x/θ). Given I(θ) = 1/θ², give the Cramér–Rao bound for unbiased estimators of θ and say whether x̄ attains it.
options: θ²/n, and x̄ attains it exactly
θ/n, and x̄ does not attain it
θ²/n, and x̄ does not attain it
items.explanation: The bound is 1/(nI(θ)) = θ²/n. For this family Var(X) = θ², so Var(X̄) = θ²/n, equal to the bound — x̄ is efficient. Contrast this with the RATE parameterisation of the same family, where nothing unbiased attains the floor: attainability depends on which parameter you are estimating.
items.check: The bound is the reciprocal of nI(θ), so with I = 1/θ² it is θ²/n and not 1/(nθ²). Writing the reciprocal the wrong way round is the slip option B is built from.

items.stem: To find the Cramér–Rao bound for an unbiased estimator of g(θ), arrange these steps in order.
items.explanation: Check regularity first — if the support depends on θ there is no bound to compute and everything after is wasted. Then get I₁(θ) from the second derivative, scale to nI₁ and divide [g′(θ)]² by it, and finally compare with the candidate estimator's variance to settle attainment.
items: B. Compare with Var(T) to decide whether the bound is attained
C. Check that the support does not depend on θ

items.stem: The Cramér–Rao bound gives a lower bound on:
options: the bias of any estimator of θ
the variance of the maximum likelihood estimator only
the variance of any unbiased estimator of θ, under regularity conditions
the mean squared error of every estimator, biased or not
items.explanation: The standard form is a floor on the variance of UNBIASED estimators, and it needs the regularity conditions. A biased estimator has a different bound, with (1+b′(θ))² on top, and its variance can sit below the unbiased floor — which is why the inequality says nothing about every estimator at once.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₅₀ are iid Bernoulli(p) with p = 0.5. Give Iₙ(p) and the Cramér–Rao bound for unbiased estimators of p.
items.explanation: I₁(p) = 1/(p(1−p)) = 1/0.25 = 4, so Iₙ = 50(4) = 200 and the bound is 1/200 = 0.005. Check it against Var(x̄) = p(1−p)/n = 0.25/50 = 0.005 — equal, so x̄ is efficient here.
items.check: The bound and the total information are reciprocals. If the two numbers do not multiply to 1, one of them is wrong.

items.stem: Consider Fisher information.
items.explanation: A is true — information adds over independent observations. B is true, and is the identity that makes the second form usable. C is false: I(θ) = −E[∂²ℓ/∂θ²] is the EXPECTED information, a function of θ; evaluating −∂²ℓ/∂θ² at θ̂ gives the OBSERVED information, a number from one dataset. D is true — a zero or negative information signals an algebra error, since I(θ) = Var(score) ≥ 0 and the conditions require it strictly positive.
statements: Iₙ(θ) = n I₁(θ) for an iid sample.
I(θ) is computed by evaluating the second derivative at the MLE.

A.why: Independence makes the information in the sample the sum of the individual contributions.

B.why: The information identity, itself a consequence of differentiating under the integral.

C.why: That is the OBSERVED information. The bound uses the expected version.

D.why: It is a variance, and the regularity conditions require 0 < I(θ) < ∞.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₉ are iid N(μ, σ²) with σ² = 36 known. An unbiased estimator T of μ has Var(T) = 8. Give the Cramér–Rao bound and the efficiency of T.
items.explanation: I₁(μ) = 1/σ² = 1/36, so Iₙ = 9/36 = 0.25 and the bound is 1/0.25 = 4, which is also σ²/n = 36/9 = 4. Efficiency is CRLB/Var(T) = 4/8 = 0.5, so T carries half the information X̄ does. Option A takes the ratio upside down.
items.check: Efficiency is bound ÷ variance and can never exceed 1. Any answer above 1 means the ratio was inverted.

items.stem: An unbiased estimator T of θ is found with Var(T) strictly below 1/(nI(θ)). What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing — T is simply a very good estimator
T must be biased after all
Either the regularity conditions fail, or there is an arithmetic error — no unbiased estimator can beat the bound where it applies
The Fisher information was computed for the wrong sample size
items.explanation: Where the conditions hold, the inequality is a theorem: nothing unbiased can sit below the floor. A result below it is evidence that a condition was violated — most often a support that moves with θ — or that the arithmetic is wrong. U(0,θ) is the standard case where quoting the bound produces exactly this contradiction.

items.stem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Bernoulli(p). Find the Cramér–Rao bound for unbiased estimators of the variance g(p) = p(1−p), and evaluate it at p = 0.4, n = 25.
items.explanation: g′(p) = 1 − 2p, so [g′(p)]² = (1−2p)². With I(p) = 1/(p(1−p)) the bound is [g′(p)]²/(nI(p)) = (1−2p)²p(1−p)/n. At p = 0.4: (0.2)² = 0.04 and p(1−p) = 0.24, so the bound is 0.04 × 0.24/25 = 0.0096/25 = 0.000384. Option A is the bound for p itself rather than for p(1−p); option C drops the square on the derivative.
items.check: The derivative is SQUARED and the bound is a quotient, not a product. Note also that at p = 0.5 the bound is zero, because g′(0.5) = 0 — the variance is at its maximum there and locally flat.

items.stem: Consider efficiency and attainment of the bound.
items.explanation: A is true — efficiency is the ratio of the floor to the achieved variance. B is false: the MLE's efficiency is an asymptotic statement, and at finite n the MLE may be biased and sit above the floor. C is true, and is the exact attainment criterion. D is true — for the exponential rate the UMVUE has variance λ²/(n−2) against a floor of λ²/n.
statements: e(T) = CRLB/Var(T), and T is efficient when e(T) = 1.
Every maximum likelihood estimator is efficient at every sample size.
The bound is attained exactly when the score factorises as A(θ)[T − g(θ)].
A UMVUE can have variance strictly above the Cramér–Rao bound.

A.why: The definition, and the ratio is at most 1.

B.why: Asymptotic only. At finite n the MLE is often biased and above the floor.

C.why: The equality case of the Cauchy–Schwarz step — the score must be linear in T.

D.why: λ²/(n−2) > λ²/n. Best unbiased and efficient are different achievements.

items.stem: X₁,…,X₄₀ are iid Exponential with mean θ = 5. Give the Cramér–Rao bound for unbiased estimators of θ, and the efficiency of x̄.
items.explanation: For the mean parameterisation I(θ) = 1/θ², so the bound is θ²/n = 25/40 = 0.625. Var(X̄) = θ²/n = 0.625 as well, so x̄ attains it and its efficiency is exactly 1. The rate parameterisation of the same family behaves differently — there nothing unbiased attains the floor.
items.check: Attainment depends on which parameter you are estimating, not on the family. For the exponential MEAN it is attained; for the RATE it is not.

items.stem: Which quantity does the Cramér–Rao bound use?
options: the score evaluated at the MLE
the second derivative of the likelihood, not the log-likelihood
items.explanation: The bound is stated with the expected information, an average over all the samples that might have been drawn and a function of θ. The observed information is a single number computed from the data in hand; software often reports it, and questions exploit the difference.

items.stem: To decide whether an unbiased estimator T of θ is efficient, arrange these steps.
items.explanation: Check regularity first — if the support depends on θ there is no bound to compare against and the question is void. Then compute I(θ) and the bound 1/(nI(θ)), then Var(T), and finally take the ratio to get the efficiency.
items: A. Compute I(θ) and form the bound 1/(nI(θ))
D. Check the regularity conditions hold
